title: The
Fragile Middle
slides.dek: A network with a tipping point is most vulnerable not when it is most connected, but in between. Raise the wiring and a system-wide cascade first becomes possible, then impossible. The danger lives in a window in the middle.

slides.body: Take Duncan Watts' 2002 rule: you adopt once the *fraction* of your neighbours who have adopted reaches some threshold. Set it at a fifth. Count your friends. With four, a single one is already a quarter, past the bar, so *one* convert is enough to tip you. With twenty, one friend is only five percent, and you sit unmoved. The people a single neighbour can tip are exactly the ones with few enough connections, degree at most five here. Call them *vulnerable*. They are the only nodes a spreading front recruits for free: a well-connected node never moves on one early adopter. The vulnerable are the road a cascade travels.

So the real question is not how many nodes are vulnerable but whether they *connect*. A spark walks vulnerable node to vulnerable node; strewn into little islands, the fire burns one and dies, but fused into one *giant vulnerable component*, a single seed dropped anywhere runs the whole network. It is the giant component from drop #045 wearing a mask, and it does what the plain giant never did: it appears, and then it *disappears*. Dial connectivity up on a fixed 140-node board and the giant swells from a dozen nodes to 122, then dissolves back to eight, as almost everyone gets too many friends to be swayed by one.

three modules over one idea: a live 140-node board colouring the giant vulnerable component as average degree climbs, a precomputed cascade window at n=250/2000 (two-humped, zero at both ends), and the branching curve z*Pr[Poisson(z)<=K*-2] against one, both crossings marked

checked offline then re-read live in a browser (SSR === client): window edges z in [1.021, 5.765] at phi=0.20 / K*=5; the vulnerable giant runs 12 -> 122 -> 8 as z climbs, browser read back z=3 -> 122/140 (87.1%), z=6 -> 12 (8.6%). contrast: 0 fails, light + dark

slides.big:
too sparse to spread,
too dense to sway,
*fragile in between.*
slides.sub: Dial the connectivity of a 140-node graph and watch the giant vulnerable component appear then dissolve, ice for the connected spine of easily-swayed nodes, ember for the ones too wired to tip. Then run the window over thousands of fresh graphs: the fraction that a single random seed can tip traces a two-humped curve, zero at both ends, alive only in the middle. The last panel draws Watts' branching criterion crossing one at both edges, average degree from about 1.02 to 5.77, the exact boundary between too sparse to spread and too dense to sway. Recomputed live from a seeded generator, zero external data.
